subject: medicine
title: Urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, and nephrolithiasis types

steps.tx: Ascending colonization of the lower urinary tract mucosa by uropathogenic enteric flora provokes localized superficial bladder inflammation. Clinically diagnosed as acute uncomplicated **Cystitis**, patients present with classic lower urinary symptoms: dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort in the complete absence of systemic fever or costovertebral flank pain. Uropathogenic **Escherichia coli** accounts for over seventy-five to eighty percent of episodes, utilizing specialized pyelonephritis-associated pili (P-fimbriae) to adhere avidly to uroepithelial cell surface receptors. First-line empirical antimicrobial therapy includes oral nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin trometamol, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
steps.say: Ascending colonization of the bladder by enteric bacteria causes localized superficial urinary tract inflammation. Clinically diagnosed as acute uncomplicated Cystitis, patients experience dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort without fever or flank tenderness. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli causes eighty percent of episodes, treated effectively with nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

vis.alt: Bacterial adherence and mucosal inflammatory cascade in acute cystitis.
vis.caption: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli adherence and lower urinary tract mucosal inflammation. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Invasion of the renal parenchymal tissue by ascending luminal bacteria precipitates severe suppurative tubulointerstitial inflammation accompanied by systemic illness. Presenting as **acute pyelonephritis**, patients classically exhibit a clinical triad of high spiking fever with rigors, costovertebral angle tenderness (Murphy punch sign), and prominent nausea or vomiting. Microscopic inspection of unspun freshly voided urine sediment confirms white blood cell casts, providing pathognomonic diagnostic localizing evidence of active intrarenal infection. Outpatient therapy employs oral fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin, whereas hospitalized patients require intravenous third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone.
steps.say: Invasion of kidney parenchyma by ascending bacteria triggers severe suppurative inflammation accompanied by systemic infection. Presenting as acute pyelonephritis, patients exhibit high spiking fevers with rigors, costovertebral flank tenderness, and nausea. Urine microscopy confirms white blood cell casts localizing infection to the kidney, requiring antibiotic therapy with fluoroquinolones or ceftriaxone.

left.title: Acute Cystitis
points: Superficial mucosal bladder inflammation
Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain
Absence of fever, chills, or costovertebral angle tenderness
Urine sediment shows pyuria and bacteriuria; no casts

right.title: Acute Pyelonephritis
points: Suppurative renal parenchymal and pelvic infection
High spiking fever, rigors, nausea, flank pain
Prominent costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion
Pathognomonic white blood cell casts on urine microscopy

steps.tx: Documenting significant bacterial colony counts in voided urine without overt symptoms represents a common finding. Defining **asymptomatic bacteriuria** requires isolation of one hundred thousand colony-forming units per millilitre of a single bacterial species in clean-catch urine. Guidelines strictly advise against screening or antibiotic treatment in healthy women, diabetic patients, and elderly institutionalized individuals, as therapy provides no clinical benefit and selects for resistant strains. Mandatory treatment indications are restricted strictly to pregnancy and prior to urological procedures breaching mucosal barriers.
steps.say: Documenting significant bacterial counts in urine without symptoms represents a common clinical finding. Defining asymptomatic bacteriuria requires isolation of one hundred thousand colony-forming units in clean-catch urine. Antibiotic therapy is avoided in healthy, elderly, or diabetic patients to prevent antimicrobial resistance. Mandatory treatment is restricted strictly to pregnant individuals and patients undergoing invasive urological surgery.

rows: Prevents maternal pyelonephritis, preterm birth, and low birthweight
Prevents post-operative mucosal bacteraemia and severe urosepsis
Do NOT screen; Do NOT treat
No reduction in symptomatic UTI; induces antimicrobial resistance
Remove or replace catheter; treat only if systemic symptoms develop

steps.tx: Severe necrotizing infections and persistent atypical suppurative processes produce distinct morphological variants of complicated pyelonephritis. Developing **emphysematous pyelonephritis** constitutes a life-threatening, gas-producing parenchymal necrosis occurring almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetic patients, demonstrating parenchymal gas on non-contrast computed tomography. In contrast, **xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis** features chronic suppurative destruction of renal parenchyma replaced by lipid-laden foamy macrophages, classically associated with Proteus staghorn calculi. When persistent pyuria coincides with negative routine bacterial cultures, investigating for **sterile pyuria** is mandatory to rule out genitourinary tuberculosis, Chlamydia, interstitial cystitis, or analgesic nephropathy.
steps.say: Severe necrotizing infections produce distinct morphological variants of complicated pyelonephritis. Developing emphysematous pyelonephritis is a life-threatening gas-forming necrosis occurring almost exclusively in diabetics, showing parenchymal gas on computed tomography. In contrast, xanthogranulomatous disease demonstrates granulomatous destruction with lipid-laden foamy macrophages, while sterile pyuria mandates testing for genitourinary tuberculosis.

left.title: Emphysematous Pyelonephritis
points: Severe acute necrotizing infection with parenchymal gas
Occurs almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetics
E. coli and Klebsiella ferment tissue glucose into CO2
Emergency broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and drainage

right.title: Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis (XPN)
points: Chronic unilateral destructive granulomatous mass
Lipid-laden foamy macrophages (xanthoma cells)
Strong association with obstructing Proteus staghorn calculi
Mimics renal cell carcinoma clinically and on imaging

steps.tx: Acute intraluminal obstruction of the ureter by migrating crystalline concretions precipitates dramatic proximal capsular distension and smooth muscle spasm. Experiencing acute **renal colic** produces sudden, excruciating, unremitting flank pain radiating along the dermatomal distribution of the ureter toward the ipsilateral groin, testicle, or labium majorum. Patients appear characteristically restless, pacing continuously to find a comfortable position. Non-contrast low-dose computed tomography of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (CT KUB) represents the diagnostic gold standard, rapidly identifying stone size, location, and secondary signs of obstruction like hydroureter and perinephric stranding.
steps.say: Acute obstruction of the ureter by migrating kidney stones causes severe proximal capsular distension and muscle spasm. Experiencing acute renal colic produces sudden excruciating flank pain radiating into the groin or testicle. Patients appear characteristically restless, pacing continuously for relief, with non-contrast computed tomography providing rapid diagnostic confirmation.

vis.alt: Abdominal radiograph demonstrating radio-opaque ureteric calculus causing acute renal colic.
vis.caption: Radio-opaque ureteric calculus lodged at the vesicoureteric junction causing acute renal colic. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Supersaturation of urinary solute precursors leads to crystal nucleation, aggregation, and stone formation within the calyces. Comprising over seventy-five to eighty percent of all urinary calculi, **calcium oxalate stones** appear radio-opaque on conventional radiographs, displaying distinctive envelope-shaped (dihydrate) or dumbbell-shaped (monohydrate) crystals on urine microscopy. Idiopathic **hypercalciuria** with completely normal serum calcium represents the single most common metabolic predisposing abnormality. Hyperoxaluria secondary to malabsorptive states (such as Crohn disease or bariatric surgery, where unabsorbed fatty acids saponify calcium, leaving free oxalate for excessive colonic absorption) dramatically accelerates calcium oxalate precipitation.
steps.say: Supersaturation of urinary solutes causes crystal nucleation and stone formation within the renal calyces. Comprising eighty percent of all stones, calcium oxalate stones appear radio-opaque on radiographs, displaying envelope-shaped crystals on microscopy. Idiopathic hypercalciuria with normal blood calcium represents the commonest metabolic risk factor, while enteric fat malabsorption dramatically increases dietary oxalate uptake.

left.title: Calcium Oxalate Stones
points: Most common urinary stone type (75% to 80%)
Radio-opaque on plain KUB radiographs
Envelope or dumbbell-shaped crystals under polarized light
Driven by hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, and hypocitraturia

right.title: Preventive Dietary & Medical Strategy
points: Maintain vigorous fluid intake (>2.5 to 3 L/day)
Thiazide diuretics (Chlorthalidone) promote tubular Ca reabsorption
Potassium citrate raises urinary pH and binds free calcium
Maintain normal dietary calcium (avoid calcium restriction)

steps.tx: Infection with urea-hydrolyzing bacterial pathogens creates an intensely alkaline urinary microenvironment that drives precipitation of large branched crystalline concretions. Known as infection stones or triple phosphate, **struvite stones** are composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate combined with carbonate apatite. Uropathogens producing the enzyme urease (predominantly Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Providencia) split urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, driving urine pH above seven point two. These calculi rapidly enlarge to form massive branched staghorn calculi that fill the renal pelvis and calyces, requiring complete surgical clearance via percutaneous nephrolithotomy.
steps.say: Infection with urea-splitting bacteria creates an alkaline urinary environment that drives stone precipitation. Known as infection stones, struvite stones consist of magnesium ammonium phosphate and carbonate apatite. Urease-producing bacteria like Proteus split urea into ammonia, raising urine pH above seven. These stones expand rapidly to form massive staghorn calculi filling the renal pelvis, requiring complete surgical removal.

vis.alt: Abdominal radiograph showing a large radio-opaque staghorn calculus filling the pelvicalyceal system.
vis.caption: Radio-opaque struvite staghorn calculus filling the left pelvicalyceal system. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Distinct chemical classes of non-calcium nephrolithiasis display unique solubility curves that direct targeted medical dissolution. Forming in persistently acidic urine (pH under five point five), **uric acid stones** are radiolucent on conventional plain X-rays but visible on computed tomography, displaying pleomorphic diamond-shaped crystals. Medical dissolution with oral potassium citrate alkalinizes urine above six point five. Conversely, **cystine stones** result from inherited mutations in dibasic amino acid transporters (SLC3A1/SLC7A9), displaying pathognomonic hexagonal crystals on microscopy, requiring aggressive urinary alkalinization and tiopronin therapy.
steps.say: Distinct chemical classes of kidney stones have unique solubility profiles that direct medical dissolution therapies. Forming in persistently acidic urine, uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain radiographs and dissolve with potassium citrate alkalinization. In contrast, cystine stones arise from inherited dibasic amino acid transport defects, showing flat hexagonal crystals that require vigorous hydration and thiol-binding drugs.

rows: pH 5.5 to 6.8; Thiazides, fluid, potassium citrate
